Whites tend to frame affirmative action negatively and are less supportive of affirmative actions regardless of how it is framed, and SDO is a significant predictor of the tendency to employ frames that one finds to be relatively positive or negative.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the tendency of individuals to use certain frames when discussing affirmative action.
the tendency for Whites to frame affirmative action negatively and to use frames that most people find unacceptable and with how this framing is associated with SDO.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the framing of affirmative action by Whites is consistent with the notion that Whites are motivated to maintain their dominance over minorities.
SDO is a significant predictor of one's tendency to frame affirmative actions in terms that one finds to be relatively unacceptable.
Whites are less supportive of affirmative actions, and when they are in favor of it, they tend to frame affirmative action negatively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the tendency to frame affirmative actions in ways that are relatively negative versus positive is not a function of one's political orientation but is instead a function of SDO.

the tendency to employ frames that are perceived to be relatively negative or positive is not simply a function of the frames one has learned from the dominant group, but also a function of the degree to which one is motivated to maintain or challenge the existing social order.
the tendency to frame affirmative-action policies in terms that most Americans find morally unacceptable is not a product of ignorance or lack of awareness.
